selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: Density of identifiable wordplay/puns
selected.instruction: Score how much of the caption's humor is built on one or more clearly spottable puns or double meanings. 10 = the line's core joke is a clean, easily identified pun or double meaning. 0 = no wordplay of any kind is present.
selected.rationale: R09 ("chandelier season"), R52 ("circus breaker"), R40 ("hollandaise"), and R37 ("ballplayers") are all pun-built and land in dense_low_card_high, while R01, R22, and R43, all dense_high_card_low, contain no wordplay at all. This suggests the scorecard over-credits recognizable pun mechanics relative to the dense model.
member_names: Absence of filler/hedge words around the punchline
Deadpan delivery of high-stakes or absurd content
No comic signposting or announcement of the punchline

selected.name: Joke is inert as standalone text; needs the drawing to complete
selected.instruction: Score how much of the joke is withheld from the text and left to an unseen picture. 10 = read alone, the line is an unremarkable sentence with no discernible gag; it can only become funny once a drawing supplies the other half. 5 = partially self-explaining. 0 = a fully freestanding gag: the text alone states a complete joke, and an image would add nothing. Do not reward or penalize whether you personally find it funny; score only the degree of dependence on unseen material.
selected.rationale: R13 ('did we forget anything') and R49 ('did i miss anything') are nearly contentless as text yet dense_pct 0.868 / 0.907 with card_pct 0.100 / 0.081 — a criterion bank scoring text-visible joke content must floor them. The reverse pole is R33 and R59, complete stand-alone jokes with card_pct 0.797 / 0.896 and the two lowest dense values in the slice (0.059, 0.004). This single axis may account for more of the disagreement than any other.
member_names: Joke is inert as standalone text; needs the drawing to complete
Joke resolves within the line vs. requires outside inference

selected.name: Enters mid-conversation and implies an unheard prior turn
selected.instruction: Score whether the line is the second (or later) beat of an exchange rather than an opening statement. 10 = it plainly answers or continues something never shown — it begins with 'and', 'no,', 'that's because', or supplies an answer whose question the reader must reconstruct. 5 = addresses someone but starts the exchange. 0 = a self-contained opening pronouncement with no implied interlocutor turn.
selected.rationale: R18 ('and in exchange, i'll switch from the bass to the viola'), R02 ('about three years. how long have you been here'), R30 ('no, i can't help you get out of it like always...'), R56 ('that's because i am talking in a tin can') are dense_pct 0.719-0.958 with card_pct 0.032-0.219. A criterion bank reading each caption as a complete utterance has no way to credit the implied off-page turn, which is where much of these captions' work is done.
member_names: Enters mid-conversation and implies an unheard prior turn
Passes the overheard test as real human speech

selected.name: Topical-reference integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a public figure, trend, or current topic is essential to the joke’s mechanism; score 0 when it is merely name-dropped or could be removed without changing the line.
selected.rationale: R14, R18, and R25 all use Trump-related references, but the criterion distinguishes meaningful transformation from detachable topical labeling.
member_names: Not carried by a dated topical or political name-drop

selected.name: Status reversal
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the line sharply flips who has authority, leverage, knowledge, or social standing; score 0 when the interpersonal relationship remains unchanged.
selected.rationale: R04, R31, and R50 turn on altered authority or social standing, whereas R49 and R56 provide little relational movement.
member_names: Implied social/status expectation reversed within the line

selected.name: Earned detail
selected.instruction: Score 10 when each concrete detail causes or intensifies the comic turn; score 0 when details are ornamental, exhaustive, or interchangeable.
selected.rationale: The dishwasher detail in R47 and the elephant-elevator pairing in R57 materially drive their turns; the extensive seat and body-position description in R20 is more vulnerable to feeling decorative.

selected.name: Productive ambiguity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the line leaves an intriguing gap that invites a specific comic inference while remaining understandable; score 0 when it is either fully obvious or merely unclear.
selected.rationale: R02, R07, R09, and R29 withhold just enough information to make the reader mentally complete the situation.

selected.name: Semantic reframe
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary word or phrase naturally supports one reading and then snaps to another; score 0 when wording remains literal or produces a strained, unclear pun.
selected.rationale: R09, R10, R29, and R60 exploit shifts in the meanings of familiar terms, unlike more literal lines such as R07 and R37.

selected.name: Controlled escalation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise escalates to a larger consequence without abandoning the underlying situation; score 0 when the line adds an abrupt shock or unrelated pile-on.
selected.rationale: R24 and R48 escalate practical problems while preserving their situations, whereas R40 and R43 move quickly to extreme consequences with less continuity.

selected.name: Specific persona markers (named addressee or verbal tic)
selected.instruction: Score how strongly the caption signals a particular speaker's distinct voice via a named addressee, in-group term, or idiosyncratic phrasing. 10 = the line names a specific addressee or contains a clearly idiosyncratic verbal habit that only this character would use. 0 = the line is voice-neutral and could be said by anyone in any context.
selected.rationale: R33 ("we're dinosaurs, ronny... we don't do whimsy") and R38 ("that's phil from liquidations") both name a specific person and sit in dense_low_card_high, while R22 ("and now we wait") and R60 ("try not to overthink it"), both dense_high_card_low, are voice-neutral, generic lines.
member_names: Specific persona markers (named addressee or verbal tic)

selected.name: Morbid/dark content (death, injury, loss) as the comic engine
selected.instruction: Score how much the caption's humor is built directly on death, physical injury, loss, or decline. 10 = the central joke turns on dark subject matter (death, injury, loss) stated as the punchline's core content. 0 = the caption's content is entirely benign, with nothing dark or morbid.
selected.rationale: R04 ("my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg") and R10 ("don't cry, now daddy can get his full 1200 stimulus", implying a death) both anchor their humor in dark content and sit in dense_low_card_high; R29 ("this fish is dead"), dense_high_card_low, shows the same device appearing on the other side too, so isolating darkness as its own axis lets a judge credit content-darkness independent of the flat delivery captured in A01.
member_names: Morbid/dark content (death, injury, loss) as the comic engine

selected.name: Quietly reassigns power, blame, or who the subject is
selected.instruction: Score whether the line performs a reversal of standing between the parties or between speaker and their own situation. 10 = the sentence relocates authority, victimhood, or agency in a way the reader must recompute ('you now report directly to me'; 'at least i know i'm a puppet'). 5 = mild status friction. 0 = the expected character says the expected thing from the expected position.
selected.rationale: R35, R58 ('do you have any idea who you're talking to'), R01 ('at least i know i'm a puppet'), R46 ('can i get a discount? this fish is dead') carry dense_pct 0.820-0.956 against card_pct 0.004-0.264. R17's card_pct of 0.004 with dense_pct 0.913 is the extreme case: nothing in the text is 'clever' by any explicit measure, and the whole effect is a status inversion the reader completes.
member_names: Quietly reassigns power, blame, or who the subject is

selected.name: Payload is not a pun on a depicted object's name
selected.instruction: Score whether the line's comic payload rests on a homophone or double meaning of a physically depicted object. 10 = no such pun anywhere; the line would survive intact if the object were renamed. 4 = a pun is present but is decoration on an independent idea. 0 = the entire caption exists to deliver one word that means both a scene object and something else ('circus breaker', 'fixture', 'downsizing', 'liquidations', 'best in show'). Score the mechanism, not the cleverness of the pun.
selected.rationale: R40 ('circus breaker'), R29 ('fixture'), R53 ('downsizing'), R20 ('liquidations'), R55 ('best in show') all sit at card_pct 0.855-0.961 with dense_pct 0.110-0.186. Object-name puns are maximally legible to any explicit criterion ('uses wordplay', 'is clever with language') and are precisely what the dense model appears to discount as a stale move.
member_names: Payload is not a pun on a depicted object's name

selected.name: Institutional vocabulary reframes the stakes rather than supplying a pun
selected.instruction: Composite. First ask whether the line imports vocabulary from an institution — leases, billing, HR, litigation, parenting, medicine. If it does not, score 5. If it does: 10 = the vocabulary recasts what the scene is about, importing a whole system of obligations the picture did not have; 0 = the vocabulary is present only because one of its words literally matches something drawn, i.e. it is A03 wearing a suit.
selected.rationale: The same lexical field falls on both sides of the disagreement, so the discriminating property is the use, not the field. Reframing: R15 ('if this doesn't break our lease'), R57 ('getting rid of the lawyer is going to cost you'), R35, at dense_pct 0.901-0.994 and card_pct 0.157-0.272. Punning: R53 ('selected for downsizing'), R54 ('hidden fees from thin air'), R20 ('phil from liquidations'), at card_pct 0.804-0.926 and dense_pct 0.084-0.165. A criterion that merely detects 'domain-specific language' credits both.
member_names: Institutional vocabulary reframes the stakes rather than supplying a pun

selected.name: Pun spelled out vs. left compressed for the reader to complete
selected.instruction: Score whether a pun's second meaning is made explicit by surrounding words, versus compressed into a single word/phrase the reader must decode unaided. 10 = the sentence structure explicitly walks the reader to the pun's alternate meaning (e.g., parallel phrasing that names both senses). 0 = the pun is a single compressed word/phrase with no scaffolding, and the reader must supply the second meaning entirely on their own.
selected.rationale: R09 ("chandelier season doesn't begin until next week" — the "season" phrasing spells out the hunting pun) and R40 ("depressed around the hollandaise" — phrased to walk the reader to "holidays") are both dense_low_card_high and fully scaffolded, while R56 ("i don't trust the poles anymore"), dense_high_card_low, leaves the poles/polls pun fully compressed with no scaffolding.
member_names: Pun spelled out vs. left compressed for the reader to complete

selected.name: Named partisan political figures and outlets
selected.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption names, or unmistakably designates, a real partisan political figure, party, campaign, or news outlet. 0 = no political person, party, campaign or outlet is referenced. 5 = one such reference appears as a passing modifier. 10 = a named political figure or outlet is the caption's subject, or two or more such references appear. Judge extent of political reference only. Do NOT judge whether the reference is accurate, fair, agreeable, well-aimed, or funny, and do NOT let your own view of the figure or outlet move the score in either direction.
selected.rationale: Writing to a venue's presumed political sympathies is a social effect on reception that lives upstream of the text and is not comic craft, but it leaves an obvious lexical trace. In this slice R15 names 'marjorie taylor greene', R30 names 'the trump lure', R42 says 'if trump wins again', and R49 says 'no fox news'. All four are legible as partisan-audience alignment independent of whether the joke lands. Because shared politics can win favour from a like-minded reader for reasons that have nothing to do with the caption being a good contest entry, and because the political community a submitter belongs to is not plausibly a cause of genuine comic quality, this is tagged as a pure nuisance.
member_names: Named partisan political figures and outlets
selected.upstream_parent: the submitter's political community and the assumed politics of the venue's readership
upstream_parent_all_members: the submitter's political community and the assumed politics of the venue's readership

selected.name: Caption length / verbosity (word count, clause count)
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 how long and multi-clause this caption is, purely as a word-count/structure measure (0 = extremely terse, roughly <=6 words with a single clause; 10 = long, multi-clause with an explicit setup plus payoff). Do not judge whether the length helps or hurts the joke -- score only how much text/structure is present.
selected.rationale: dense_high_card_low items cluster around very short one-liners (R18 'did we forget anything'; R22 'and now we wait'), while dense_low_card_high items cluster around longer, multi-clause captions (R03 'she's a real beaut, don, but you'll have to throw it back...'; R37's airplane/emergency-exit bit). Length itself, not joke content, tracks the split.
member_names: Caption length / verbosity (word count, clause count)

selected.name: Institutional register
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use legal, financial, bureaucratic, corporate, or other institutional vocabulary? Judge only the register, not whether it is good.
selected.rationale: Institutional language may correlate with audience familiarity or venue conventions without representing quality. Examples include R01, R05, R13, R40, R53, and R60.
upstream_parent_all_members: submitter's occupation and professional milieu (and the venue readership's occupational skew)

selected.name: Numeric logistical specificity
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent of numerals, times, measurements, counts, locations, or other logistical specifics. Count their presence only; do not judge whether the details improve the caption.
selected.rationale: Data-like details can affect readability and memorability independently of entry quality. Examples include R14, R20, R33, and R43.

selected.name: Kinship framing and first-name familiar address
selected.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption is framed around household or family relationships, or addresses its listener by a personal first name or familiar role term. Count kinship nouns ('mom', 'dad', 'daddy', 'son', 'husband', 'wife'), possessive family references, domestic-curfew or spousal-complaint framing, and first-name vocatives. 0 = no kinship term, no family framing, and no personal name of address. 5 = one kinship term or one first-name vocative. 10 = the caption's whole premise is a family relationship, or it combines a kinship term with a name of address. Judge extent of kinship and familiar-address framing only. Do NOT judge whether the family framing is warm, tired, relatable, or well observed, and do NOT judge whether the caption is funny.
selected.rationale: A submitter's own household is invisible to the model, but it drives which relationship they reach for when inventing a speaker, and it leaves a hard lexical fingerprint. This slice is full of it: R04 says 'daddy', R13 says 'my husband', R25 says 'my mom ... my dad', R55 addresses a 'son', R39 and R43 are both spousal-curfew complaints, and R41, R53 and R34 use the first names 'don', 'ronny' and 'phil'. Compare R12, R22 and R59, which have no kinship or naming content at all. Life-stage cohort can align a caption with a similarly aged readership for reasons that are demographic rather than comic, and cohort itself is not plausibly a cause of genuine caption quality, so this is a pure nuisance.
member_names: Kinship framing and first-name familiar address
selected.upstream_parent: submitter's life stage and household composition (age cohort, parenthood, marital status)
upstream_parent_all_members: submitter's life stage and household composition (age cohort, parenthood, marital status)

selected.name: Discourse-marker hedge opener (veteran stylistic tic)
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the caption opens with a short discourse-marker or hedge phrase (e.g. 'well,', 'okay,', 'no idea,', 'at least,', 'ladies and gentlemen,') before its main statement. 0 = caption launches directly into its main statement with no such opener; 10 = caption is built entirely around a prominent framing opener. Do not judge whether the opener is skillfully used -- score only its presence.
selected.rationale: Repeat entrants to a recurring contest often develop recognizable stock framing devices; R07 opens with 'ladies and gentlemen,' and R17 opens with 'no idea,' -- these openers recur across items on both sides of the split (R07 dense_low_card_high; R17 dense_high_card_low), consistent with a submitter-style tic that a familiar community could reward independent of the specific joke's merit.
member_names: Front-loaded interjections, discourse markers, and emphatic punctuation
selected.upstream_parent: author's contest experience / seniority in the submitter community
upstream_parent_all_members: author's contest experience / seniority in the submitter community

selected.name: Question-format framing
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much is the caption phrased as a direct question or question-like exchange? Judge only the visible interrogative format, not whether it is good.
selected.rationale: Question framing may track familiar dialogue conventions without measuring caption quality. Examples include R01, R04, R07, and R10.

selected.name: Explicit lexical naming of the depicted object or setting
selected.instruction: Read only the caption text. Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption explicitly names, in words, a concrete physical object, fixture, animal, room, or vehicle that is evidently the thing being drawn, rather than referring to it only by a pronoun or leaving it unnamed. 0 = no concrete depicted object is named at all; the caption uses only pronouns, deixis ('this', 'it', 'him') or abstractions. 5 = one concrete object is named once in passing. 10 = the depicted object is named explicitly and is also the grammatical focus, or is named more than once, or is named together with its setting. Count nouns only, and count them whether or not they are used punningly. Judge extent of naming only. Do NOT judge whether naming the object is a good or bad move, whether it spoils or sharpens the joke, or whether the caption is funny.
selected.rationale: Repeat entrants learn the house habit of letting the drawing carry the referent and writing pure in-world dialogue; first-time submitters more often lexicalize what is already visible. That difference in entrant experience leaves an exact textual fingerprint: R07 and R46 both name 'chandelier' outright, R41 names 'light fixtures', R40 names 'fixture', R32 names the 'circus breaker'. Against these, R11, R28, R51 and R56 name nothing depicted at all and lean entirely on pronouns and deixis. Entrant experience is a plausibly real driver of reception that is not itself caption quality (a veteran's habit can be scored as fluency), but the same experience plausibly does also produce genuinely better jokes, so this is tagged mixed rather than pure nuisance.
member_names: Explicit lexical naming of the depicted object or setting
selected.upstream_parent: submitter's familiarity with the contest's conventions (novice one-off entrant vs. repeat veteran entrant)
upstream_parent_all_members: submitter's familiarity with the contest's conventions (novice one-off entrant vs. repeat veteran entrant)

selected.name: Fragmentary minimalism
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 for sentence fragments, very short utterances, ellipses, or highly compressed syntax. Judge only the degree of compression; do not judge whether brevity is good or funny.
selected.rationale: Very short forms may receive different processing from complete sentences while saying nothing about entry quality. Examples include R05, R08, R17, R24, and R50.

selected.name: Time-sensitive framing
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain dates, times, seasons, delays, temporary windows, or other explicitly time-bound cues? Judge only the temporal cues, not whether they are good.
selected.rationale: Submission timing can make certain temporal references more salient, while timely framing may also genuinely help construction; therefore this is a sensitivity channel. Examples include R24, R41, R57, and R59.
